1:
The seven and the plagues are read first. Victorinus and Bede give the same reason for the number, that the wrath of God always strikes the obstinate people with seven plagues, that is perfectly, as Leviticus says; both add that these are the last because in them the wrath is consummated. Bede alone identifies the seven angels with the Church, replete with sevenfold grace, and notes that the hearer is made attentive by the words great and marvellous. Robertson finds the number appropriate to finality; Ellicott warns that they are seven angels and not the seven, so that identifying them is needless. Ellicott takes the word plagues back to Egypt and distinguishes them from the trumpets: those warned men to repent, these fall on men who obstinately refused to return, being not goads to the wavering but strokes upon the hardened. Wesley alone qualifies the finality: God had borne his enemies with longsuffering and now pours out wrath to the uttermost, yet even after these plagues his wrath against other enemies does not cease.

How the vials stand to the seals and trumpets is disputed. Clarke nests them: as the seventh seal contained the seven trumpets, so the seventh trumpet contains the seven vials. Robertson sets them side by side, the Bowls parallel with the Seals and Trumpets, though closer to the preceding chapters, which he calls with Swete the drama of the long conflict between the church and the world. Ellicott argues from the word last: since there are no plagues after these, the vials, like the seals and trumpets, run up to the final consummation. Clarke adds that the Targum of Jonathan on Isaiah uses the evangelist’s very word, speaking of the phials of the cup of malediction.

The sea of glass draws the widest disagreement in the chapter, and one witness rejects what two others assert. Bede takes it for the pellucid fount of Baptism, consecrated by the fire of the Holy Ghost or made red by martyrdom, so that those who overcome the beast stand upon a baptism of fire; Victorinus says the same more briefly, of standing steadfastly in the faith upon their baptism. Gill opens by refusing that reading: not baptism, but the blood of Christ, a sea for its abundant efficacy, of glass because in it justification and pardon are clearly seen, mingled with fire because the Spirit attends its application. He offers the church washed in that blood as a second possibility, and reports that most interpreters understand the world, a sea for the multitude of its inhabitants. Henry lists three: this world, a brittle thing to be broken in pieces; the gospel covenant, in allusion to the brazen sea in which the priests washed; or the Red Sea, congealed while Israel passed through, the pillar of fire reflecting on the water so that it seemed to have fire mingled with it, suiting their song of Moses. Ellicott sets it against the sea from which the beast rose: near the throne is the calm translucent sea of God’s counsels, now clear as crystal, now ruddy with the fire of righteous indignation.

The fire is accounted for more simply by the rest. Barnes contrasts the earlier vision, where the sea was wholly clear: here a portion is red, and if a meaning may be conjectured it is that the foundation of God’s dealings is justice, figured by the glass, with wrath intermingled in the fiery part. Clarke leaves symbolism for the appearance, a spacious lucid plain around the throne from which fiery coruscations were emitted, or the reflection of light producing prismatic colours. Ellicott closes on the harps, called God’s not merely as dedicated to him but as truly his, since a life that has been a discord to the world rises into music before God, and those who would make their life a melody must first take it as a conflict.
3:
Whether the song is Moses’s own or one like it divides them. Clarke says simply that it is what Moses sang when Israel had passed the Red Sea, the same song adapted to suffering but now delivered Christians. Barnes denies the identity: not that identical song, but as Moses taught the people to celebrate their deliverance with a hymn, so the redeemed celebrate theirs in a similar manner. Gill allows two senses, either that they kept the law Moses delivered distinct from the Gospel, or rather that they sang a song like his on a like occasion; and he presses the parallel hard, making Pharaoh the picture of the pope of Rome and the destruction of the Egyptians an emblem of the ruin of antichrist. Wesley finds two songs of Moses behind the phrase, that sung after the passage of the sea and that taught to Israel before his death, but rests the name chiefly on Moses being the minister and representative of the Jewish church as Christ is of the church universal.

Whether it is one song or two is a further question. Robertson calls the song of the Lamb a separate note of victory and yet holds that there is one song and not two, reporting that Charles found the two impossible to reconcile and calling the objection needless. Ellicott treats them as parallel rather than identical: Israel stood on the margin of the Red Sea and saw the overthrow of the world-power of that day, and these saints stand by the fire-blent sea and sing over the doom of the world-powers of every age. He adds that a third song of Moses, the psalm of the man of God, would not be out of place from those made glad according to the days of their affliction. Robertson traces the words to the Old Testament, great and wonderful from the psalms, the divine title from Amos, righteous and true from Deuteronomy, and notes that the manuscripts vary between the king of the ages, of the saints and of the nations. Wesley alone analyses the structure, finding six parts answering each other in pairs: the works answered by the grace that is their spring, the ways by the coming of the nations, and the question who would not fear by the manifest judgments.

The word rendered holy is where Ellicott parts from the others. Barnes takes the clause comparatively, that God is so pure that beside him no one else is holy, and Robertson renders it that he is alone holy. Ellicott points out that the word here is not the one usually employed of God’s holiness. Applied to men it denotes one who reverences the sacred obligations of natural and moral order, apart from law or custom; applied to God, his recognition of the obligations his own character imposes on him, so that what generates a holy fear is the remembrance that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

What follows from the judgments is read forward. Barnes says the punishments would teach men to reverence God, with some awe, and that everywhere in the New Testament the destruction of this power is connected with the promise of a speedy conversion of the world. Gill looks for the same, that the Jews shall seek after Christ and the Gentiles be brought into Zion, so that the fear of the Lord will be in all places. Clarke puts it as duty: all should fear and worship this God because he is just and true and holy, and acknowledge his manifest judgments. Ellicott alone marks the tense: the song is one of anticipation, since the angels of judgment are only now going forth and God’s righteous dealings are yet to be seen, though spoken of as accomplished, their completion being a divine certainty. Robertson ends on the poetry, that this martyrs’ song has the ring of great verse.
5:
What the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony is gets four answers. Barnes restricts it, saying the word means not the whole building but the holy of holies, God’s peculiar dwelling-place, usually closed and now seen to open; Wesley says the same in three words, the holiest of all. Clarke reads it historically, of the temple which succeeded the tabernacle and contained the testimony, the two tables, Aaron’s rod, the pot of manna and the anointing oil, all witnessing to God’s miraculous interposition. Robertson prefers the wilderness tent to the Jerusalem temple, reporting that Charles calls the phrase strange and judging that the tent of witness and the tent of meeting are what is in mind. Ellicott grants that the expression sounds cumbrous but defends it, since Stephen spoke of the tabernacle of witness, well so called because it held the ark with the Law and was a perpetual witness of God’s presence; the temple of the tabernacle is thus the inner sanctuary of the heavenly true tabernacle, after whose pattern Moses fashioned his.

What the opening signifies is answered at length by Henry and sharply by Ellicott. Henry finds four things in it: that God was fulfilling the prophecies and promises of his covenant, always before him; that he was answering the prayers of his people, offered by their great high priest; that he was avenging the quarrel of his own Son, whose authority had been usurped; and that he was opening a wider door of liberty for his people to worship without fear of their enemies. Barnes takes it more narrowly, that the command to execute these purposes came directly from God himself, and Wesley that a new theatre was disclosed for the coming forth of his judgments. Ellicott turns the detail against those who are struck: these plagues are not, like the trumpets, calls to repentance but strokes on men who have rejected the very sanctuary the Lord pitched among them; out of the rejected temple the angels of wrath come, and it is ever true, he says, that out of rejected mercies the heaviest plagues are forged.

Who the angels are divides them along a familiar line. Clarke and Wesley take their emergence as proof of commission, that they were sent from God himself and had their instructions from his oracle, Wesley adding that John had seen them in heaven before they went in; Barnes says they came from the immediate presence of God. Gill goes further and makes them men, arguing from their coming out of the temple that they belong to the church of Christ and are ministers or members of churches, who will execute God’s wrath upon the beast; he notes that some copies read out of heaven.

Their dress raises a textual question and three readings of its meaning. Robertson takes the text to say they were arrayed with precious stone, pure and bright, noting that some manuscripts read linen; Ellicott takes linen as the text and the stone as the variant, comparing the prophet’s King of Tyre in Eden, whose covering was every precious stone. On what the garb means, Henry, Clarke and Wesley make it priestly: the habit of the high priest going in to enquire of God, linen being the habit of service, pure meaning unspotted and white meaning bright and shining, which Wesley says implies much more than bare innocence, the golden girdles being a token of high dignity and glorious rest. Barnes makes it angelic rather than priestly, the emblem of holiness and the common representation of heavenly inhabitants, befitting their rank and condition. Ellicott makes it neither, but christological: the angels are clad in a garb resembling that of Christ himself, since they come forth to do his bidding and are clothed in raiment that indicates their righteous errand.
7:
Who the living creatures are draws three answers. Gill makes them the ministers of the Gospel, this one the first of the four, like a lion for fortitude and with a voice as the noise of thunder, fitly representing those who shall give out the vials; he refuses two identifications by name, Lord Napier’s with the evangelist Luke and Grotius’s with Peter, and holds that no particular person is designed but a set of ministers. Barnes takes them for the great principles of the divine government, and finds a propriety in their concern with events so bound up with the honour of God, though which of the four is not said. Ellicott makes them creation itself, so that the wrath of God visits the rebellious through the created order, being simply the operation of his righteous law against sin.

What the vessels are is a matter of translation. Barnes objects that the Greek means a bowl or goblet having more breadth than depth, whereas our vial means a thin long bottle of glass; and he takes the image from ancient punishment, a drinking cup filled with poison and given to a man to drink. Wesley says the same of the shape, and finds the terror of the verse in the closing words, that the wrath is the wrath of him who lives for ever and ever. Ellicott and Robertson identify them by their ordinary use, the shallow saucers for incense, Robertson adding that here they are full not of incense but of wrath.

The smoke that fills the temple is read four ways. Clarke keeps closest to the precedents: the tabernacle was so filled when Moses consecrated it and the temple when Solomon did, so that this account seems partly copied from those; and he adds a second, that the high priest carried in smoking incense which filled the place with darkness and kept him from examining its ornaments too attentively, producing an air of majesty; Calmet thought the allusion might be here. Wesley points to the same precedents but adds a third: the cloud of glory was a sign of protection when the tabernacle was erected and the temple dedicated, but in the judgment of Korah the glory appeared when he and his companions were swallowed up, so that the emblem is as proper to judgment as to favour, both proceeding from the same power. Ellicott finds a nearer parallel. It is smoke here and not cloud, and the vision that answers to it is Isaiah’s, where the house was filled with smoke and the people had trifled with convictions, so that henceforth the words of God’s servants would harden rather than awaken them; the drift here is the same, the days of warning over and the sanctuary that was opened as a refuge now closed. Robertson calls it a smoke screen to keep all out of the sanctuary.

Gill offers two readings and rules out a third. It is not the smoke of false doctrine and superstition, which comes out of the bottomless pit, since this comes from God, and the churches will grow purer while the vials are poured out. It may rather be judicial blindness and hardness of heart falling on the antichristian party, so that they are not reformed by the plagues nor repent but blaspheme God; or else God’s gracious presence in his church, in allusion to the cloud that filled the tabernacle so Moses could not enter. On the exclusion Barnes is most explicit: none would be permitted to enter and make intercession, for the purpose of punishment had been formed and would certainly be executed, so that the mercy-seat was for the time inaccessible. Wesley notes that not even those who ordinarily stood before God could go into the inmost part, and that these plagues did not take up a long time as the trumpets did but followed each other swiftly.
